claims.text: Increasing noble-metal content enhances interatomic cohesion in multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
Enhanced interatomic cohesion retards high-temperature surface diffusion.
Increasing noble-metal content reduces elemental segregation during high-temperature exposure.
Increasing noble-metal content preserves a single-phase solid-solution structure at 773–1173 K better than low noble-metal content.
Noble-metal content can be varied while holding synthesis method, cooling rate, temperature profile, and support constant.
Phase homogeneity and elemental segregation can be assessed as structural mediators of stability.
Higher noble-metal content increases cohesive energy among the constituent atoms.
Higher cohesive energy reduces atomic mobility at high temperatures.
Lower noble-metal content provides less bonding stabilization.
Reduced bonding stabilization promotes elemental segregation and phase separation during high-temperature exposure.
Rapid cooling can produce homogeneous multi-element alloy nanoparticles without aggregation, elemental segregation, or phase separation.
Changing synthesis cooling rates may modify structural-stability outcomes.
Support interactions may modify nanoparticle thermal-stability outcomes.
Particle size may modify the effect of noble-metal content on stability.
The proposed noble-metal stabilization effect may not extend to substantially higher temperatures or different atmospheres.
Greater phase homogeneity and reduced segregation will lead to improved catalytic stability and performance.
Low-noble-metal baseline nanoparticles are expected to show more segregation and phase instability under catalytic service conditions.
Defective turbostratic graphite can stabilize nanoparticles through nucleation sites, partial intercalation, and high-energy anchoring at edge planes.
